# My Van Almost Caught Fire. Here's What the Electrician Found.

This isn't a fun post, and it isn't the one I planned to write this week. But a few of you are thinking about a van build, and one of you (Tasha, I'm looking at you) is about to put down a deposit, so I'm going to write it all out properly.

Short version: on Wednesday, October 28, the main cable running from my batteries to my inverter overheated and melted while I was drying a dog. Nobody was hurt, including the dog. The van is off the road for at least three weeks, and I've had a lot of time to think about what went wrong.

A big caveat before I get into it: **I am not an electrician.** I'm a dog groomer. Everything technical below comes from what an actual electrician showed and told me, plus me double-checking the math. I'll say who's saying what. If you take one thing from this post, it should be "have a professional look at your van," not "Kennedy said it's fine."

## What happened

It was about 2:15 in the afternoon, in a client's driveway in Bedford. I was drying Moose, a Bernese mountain dog, with the dryer on high. If you've never dried a Bernese, picture a lot of dog and a lot of coat, so this isn't a quick job. The dryer had been running a while.

First I smelled hot plastic. I assumed it was the dryer motor, because that's the thing that usually smells a bit hot when it's working hard. Then I saw smoke coming out of the bench seat where the batteries live.

I hit the battery switch, which kills the power. I got Moose out the side door still damp. He was honestly thrilled, because to him this was just a bonus walk. I used the fire extinguisher a bit, though I'm not even sure I needed to by that point. When I finally looked, the lug on the positive end of the cable (the metal connector on the end) was black, and the plastic jacket had melted back about 3 cm.

Moose's mom brought me a coffee and sat with me on her front steps while I shook. I'm not going to forget that. Everyone's fine. The van is not.

## My setup

Here's what's in the van, so you can see why this matters:

- A 3000W inverter. This is the box that turns battery power (12V) into regular wall-outlet power, so I can run a dryer and tools.
- Two 200Ah lithium batteries, running at 12V.
- A water heater that sometimes runs on the same system.
- Built by Coastline Van Fitouts (Darren) in spring 2025.

I'll be straight about why I picked this build: it looked great. Tidy, clean, everything labelled and neat. I trusted it because it looked professional. I'll come back to that.

## What the electrician found

After the fire I called Priya at Sackville Marine Electric. She came out, went through the whole system, and walked me through what she found. There were four main problems, and none of them would have been obvious to me looking at the van.

### 1. The cable was too thin

The cable between the battery and the inverter was **4 AWG**. Priya said for a 3000W inverter at 12V, it should have been **2/0** ("two-aught").

Cable sizing is a little backwards. The *smaller* the AWG number, the *thicker* the cable. A 2/0 is a lot thicker than a 4. By my math it has more than three times the copper in it, which is the whole point. More copper means the electricity has more room to flow without heating the cable up.

Here's the part that made it click for me. Power in watts divided by voltage gives you amps. At 12V, that adds up quickly:

- My dryer pulls roughly 1800 to 2000 watts. That's about **150 to 170 amps** at 12V, and a bit more once you count what the inverter wastes.
- When the water heater kicks in as well, the total can reach **150 to 250 amps**.
- A 3000W inverter running flat out is 250 amps by itself (3000 ÷ 12).

That's a *huge* amount of current compared to what you'd see in a house. In a house, a normal outlet circuit runs at 120V, so the same dryer would draw around 15 to 17 amps. Low voltage means high amps, and high amps need fat cable. As I understand it, the 4 AWG that was in my van is good for well under what my dryer was pulling.

One more thing Priya explained that I want to pass along: heat in a cable doesn't increase in a straight line with current. It goes up with the *square* of it. So when a cable is undersized and you push more through it, it doesn't just get a bit warmer, it gets a lot warmer, fast. That's how a cable that works fine on a light load can quietly cook itself when you ask it for real work. And groomers ask for real work, for long stretches, over and over. We're pretty much the worst-case user for a van's electrical system.

### 2. The lug was crimped wrong

A "lug" is the metal end that gets attached to the cable so it can bolt onto a battery terminal or the inverter. To attach it, you squeeze it onto the cable with a tool called a crimper, and a proper crimper for heavy cable is a serious piece of equipment that applies a lot of even pressure.

The lug on the positive end of my cable had been crimped with what looked like pliers, or possibly a hammer. Priya wasn't sure which. That kind of crimp doesn't grip evenly, which means a poor electrical connection. And a poor connection at high current gets hot, because all that resistance turns into heat right at that spot.

And here's the sneaky part: there was **heat-shrink tubing over the top of it**. That's the neat black plastic sleeve that makes a connection look finished and professional. It also meant I couldn't see the crimp at all. If I'd ever looked at that connection, it would have looked perfect.

### 3. The fuse was too far from the battery

I had a 300A ANL fuse. A fuse is the safety piece. It's supposed to blow and cut the circuit if something goes badly wrong, like a short.

The problem was where it was mounted: about **90 cm from the battery**. Priya said it should be within about **18 cm**. (That's roughly 7 inches. If you're reading a US guide, they'll say 7 inches.)

Why it matters: a fuse can only protect the wire *after* it. Anything between the battery and the fuse is unprotected. If that stretch of cable shorts, the fuse can't do anything about it, because the current never passes through the fuse on its way to the problem. Lithium batteries can put out a staggering amount of current, so you want that unprotected stretch to be as short as you can possibly make it.

I'd also like to ask Priya more about how that 300A fuse relates to the cable that was in the van, because it seems to me a fuse that large would never blow before a thin cable started to cook. I'll update this post if I get a clear answer. Either way, "right fuse, right place, right cable" is a package. They have to match each other.

### 4. No smoke detector where I actually work

The only smoke detector in the van was the one in the cab, which came with the van. There was nothing in the back, where the batteries, the inverter, and I all spend the day. I noticed the fire because I smelled it. That's luck.

## The photo that stuck with me

This is the part I keep thinking about. Priya pulled up the photos I took of the damage and put them next to thermal camera pictures from her own van, running the same kind of load.

Her van barely gets warm. Mine melted.

Same kind of load, same kind of work. The only real difference is that hers was wired for the job. When you see them side by side, it's very hard to argue with.

## What I'm not saying

I want to be fair here. I'm not trying to trash anyone publicly. I'm putting the facts in front of you, and you can make up your own mind.

Here's what I know for sure: this is what Priya found and showed me, and these are the photos. Here's what I also know: I've sent Darren three texts and an email since this happened, and I haven't heard back. I'm sharing that because it's a fact, and because Tasha is considering a deposit with him, and she deserves to know it.

I'm not saying anyone did this on purpose. I'm saying the van looked great and was built wrong, and I couldn't tell the difference. **Tidy is not the same as right.** That's the lesson I paid for.

## How to check your own van

This section is for you, and especially for Tasha. Please read it before you give anyone money.

Everything below can be done by a non-electrician with the power **off**. Switch off your battery disconnect and your inverter first. Don't touch anything inside the electrical system with the power on. Don't start tightening or adjusting connections unless you actually know how. The point of this checklist is to *find* problems, not to fix them yourself.

**The cables**
- [ ] Find the main cable running from your battery to your inverter. Many cables have the gauge printed on the jacket. Look for something like "2/0 AWG" or "4 AWG."
- [ ] Look up your inverter's size and compare. A 3000W inverter at 12V should be on thick cable. If you've got a 3000W inverter on something that looks like a garden hose's skinny cousin, get a pro to check it.
- [ ] If you can't find any markings, ask the builder what size it is and get the answer in writing.

**The fuse**
- [ ] Find the fuse on the main battery-to-inverter line. If there isn't one, that's a big problem.
- [ ] Note the fuse's rating (it's usually printed on it, in amps).
- [ ] Measure how far it is from the battery positive terminal. Mine was about 90 cm. The target is close, around 18 cm or less.
- [ ] Ask what type of fuse it is. Priya's repair plan for me includes a Class T fuse, which is a different kind of fuse that's better suited to lithium batteries.

**The connections**
- [ ] Look at every lug (the metal ends). Do they look burnt, discoloured, or blackened? Is the plastic jacket pulled back or melted anywhere?
- [ ] Look for heat-shrink covering the lugs. It isn't automatically bad, but it hides the crimp. Ask the builder to show you photos of the crimps from *before* the heat-shrink went on, or to explain what tool they used.
- [ ] Check for any smell of hot or burnt plastic around the battery area, even a faint one.

**Safety gear**
- [ ] Do you have a smoke detector in the space where you actually work, not just the cab?
- [ ] Do you have a fire extinguisher you can reach quickly, and do you know where your battery disconnect is without having to think about it?
- [ ] Can you get out fast? I got Moose out the side door. Make sure you've got more than one way out.

## Get a cheap infrared thermometer

I picked one up at Canadian Tire for about 40 dollars. Everyone who runs a van with an inverter should own one.

An infrared thermometer is the little gun-shaped thing you point at a surface to read its temperature from a distance. Run your normal heavy load (for me, the dryer) and, carefully and from a safe distance, check the temperature of the lugs and cables. You're looking for anything that's noticeably hotter than everything around it. In a well-built system, the cables and connections stay pretty unremarkable even when the load is high.

I'll be honest about the limits. It only reads surface temperature, so it can't see inside a connection or through heat-shrink. It's one more way to catch a problem early, not a replacement for a pro looking at the whole system. If you find something hot, stop using that load and get an electrician in. I don't have a magic number for what's "too hot," and I'm not going to pretend I do.

## For Tasha, and anyone about to hire a builder

Before you pay a deposit, ask your builder for the following, **in writing**:

1. **The cable size** for every main run, especially battery to inverter, with the inverter size and battery voltage noted.
2. **The fuse type, rating, and location** for each run, including how far it is from the battery.
3. **What tool they use for crimping lugs**, and whether they'll send photos of the connections before they're covered up.
4. **A wiring diagram** of the whole system.
5. **What smoke detectors and fire safety gear** will be in the living and working space.

A good builder will answer all of this without any trouble. If you get vague answers, or a "don't worry about it," that tells you something too.

And if you can swing it, pay a marine or RV electrician to inspect the finished build *before* you hand over the final payment. Priya's rate for an inspection would've been a fraction of what this is costing me now.

I realize that sounds like a lot to ask of someone who's just trying to build a business. It is. But it's a lot less than what I'm dealing with.

## Where I'm at

It's been a rough couple of weeks, and I'll just say it plainly: I'm scared. This van is my whole income. Rent is still due on the 1st whether the van runs or not.

The repair quote is **$4,200**. That covers rewiring the main runs, a new fuse block, and a Class T fuse. It'll take **three weeks at a minimum**, and the parts are on order. In the meantime I've had to cancel **31 appointments so far**, and that number's going to keep climbing. I hate every one of those calls. These are clients I've built up over time, and their dogs are the best part of my job.

Insurance has said "maybe." An adjuster is coming Thursday, and I'm trying not to build my hopes up or down until I hear what they say.

I'm taking it one day at a time. I'm lucky to have people around me, from Moose's mom and her coffee to Priya, who has been patient and clear, and to all of you who've sent messages.

I'll post again when the van's back on the road, with the real final numbers and how the repair went. If any of you have questions about the checklist, ask me and I'll pass them to Priya.

Go check your cables. Please.

---

A few things for you before you post it:

- **Timing:** Your notes said "last week," but the fire was Oct 28 and today is Nov 11, so it's been two weeks. I left out "last week" and just used the date. The "rent due the 1st" line is also vague on purpose, since Nov 1 has already passed.
- **The fuse paragraph:** The point that a 300A fuse wouldn't protect a thin 4 AWG cable is my own reasoning, not something Priya told you. I flagged it in the post as a question for her. Confirm it with her before publishing, or cut it. The same goes for "4 AWG is good for well under what the dryer pulled." I kept it vague, but it's worth asking her for an actual number.
- **Naming Darren and Coastline:** I named them since you want Tasha to see it, and I stuck to facts Priya found plus the unanswered messages. With an insurance claim open, it's worth asking the adjuster on Thursday whether they'd rather you hold off on naming anyone. It's easy to swap in "my builder" if you'd rather.
- **Class T fuse:** I described it as "better suited to lithium batteries," which is general knowledge and not something from your notes. Ask Priya if she'd phrase it differently.
